site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: The Name That Lifted Ajamila Home
stories.source: Srimad Bhagavatam · Canto 6, Chapter 1 (Ajamilopakhyana), Bhaktivedanta VedaBase translation
body: In the city of Kanyakubja, the brahmin Ajamila had drifted far from his early vows, fathering ten children by a servant girl. Yet when his youngest son was born, he named the little one Narayana, never knowing what mercy lived in those syllables.

On his deathbed, three Yamadutas rose to drag his soul away, and terror broke from his lips as he called for his boy, Narayana. At that sound, four golden four-armed Vishnudutas blazed into the room and forbade the messengers of death to touch him.

Ajamila wept and turned back to God, journeying to Haridwar to live his final days in remembrance. When his hour came again, the Vishnudutas carried him home to the spiritual world, the holy name having saved him even when he had not meant to speak it.

stories.title: Kabandha Lifts His Curse in Flame
stories.source: Valmiki Ramayana · Aranya Kanda, Sarga 69-72 (Gita Press translation)
body: Deep in the Dandaka forest, Rama and Lakshmana came upon a fearsome being without a head, a single eye set in his belly. He was Kabandha, the gandharva Danu, trapped in a monstrous shape by an old curse. He begged the brothers to free him with fire and the pouring of sacred libations.

The princes obeyed, and as the great body burned, something bright stirred within the ashes. A radiant gandharva rose from the flames, clothed in celestial light, his true form at last restored. He praised Rama for the mercy shown and shared tidings of Sita, pointing the way forward.

With his curse lifted, the luminous gandharva guided the brothers onward, telling them to seek the monkey-king Sugriva at Rishyamuka. A blessing hidden inside a trial was revealed, and the path to hope grew clearer beneath the forest canopy.

stories.title: Bharata's Vow at Chitrakuta
stories.source: Valmiki Ramayana · Ayodhya Kanda, Sarga 99 (Gita Press translation)
body: When King Dasharatha passed away, Prince Bharata crossed the Ganges with a heart too heavy for a throne. He found Rama dwelling in the forest at Chitrakuta and fell weeping at his brother's feet, begging him to return and be crowned king of Ayodhya.

Rama would not break their father's word, so Bharata asked only for his paduka. Lifting Rama's sandals onto his head with the reverence due a king, Bharata walked home and set them upon the throne, ruling Ayodhya as regent in his brother's name.
For fourteen long years, Bharata governed with the sandals before him, fasting and sleeping on the bare ground, faithful to the moment Rama would come home again.

stories.title: The Bharunda Birds' Lesson
stories.source: Panchatantra · Book 2, 'The Winning of Friends', The Bharunda Birds — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
body: In a quiet grove, two strange birds called the Bharunda shared one body and two heads. One craved the cool lotus stalks from the pond, the other longed for the silver fish swimming beneath the water. Their quarrel grew hotter with each passing moment, until one head, unable to resist, swallowed the other's chosen feast.

But the shared body, fed on conflict instead of kindness, began to weaken and sicken. Both heads, bound to the same fate, felt the poison of their stubbornness and nearly perished together in the dust. Their single heart could not survive the war of two wills.

A wise ascetic wandering past saw their suffering and gently spoke. He taught the Bharunda that a partnership of unequals is doomed to crumble, and that a true friend guards another's life as dearly as their own. Hearing this, the two heads softened, finding in compassion the simple hope of staying whole.

stories.title: Jambu the Parrot's Gentle Wisdom
stories.source: The Jataka · Vol. V, Tesakuna Jataka (No. 521), E. B. Cowell ed., public domain
body: In the royal court of long ago, three eggs — a myna's, a maina's, and a parrot's — hatched in the homes of courtiers. The children were raised in princely splendor, and the old king called each of them son and daughter, warming his twilight years with their company.

When the king came to ask about righteous rule, the parrot Jambuka answered with twelve stanzas, explaining the five royal powers and the duties of a king. Delighted, the king appointed the wise bird his commander-in-chief, trusting feathered counsel above all others.

After the king passed, Jambuka gently refused the throne, guiding the people instead toward righteousness before returning home to the forest — leaving behind a kingdom steadier in virtue than it had been when he found it.
